knowledge_statements.scope_note: One iteration for a standard-form minimization LP, including reduced-cost optimality testing, an unbounded-ray test, and the minimum-ratio basis exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), given a basis partition \((\mathcal B,\mathcal N)\) with nonsingular \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\), \(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b\geq0\), and \(x_{\mathcal N}=0\), solve \(B^T\lambda=c_{\mathcal B}\) and compute \(s_{\mathcal N}=c_{\mathcal N}-N^T\lambda\). If \(s_{\mathcal N}\geq0\), stop at an optimal point. Otherwise choose \(q\in\mathcal N\) with \(s_q<0\), solve \(Bd=A_q\), and stop as unbounded if \(d\leq0\). If some \(d_i>0\), set \(\theta=\min_{i:d_i>0}(x_{\mathcal B})_i/d_i\), choose a minimizing position \(p\), update \(x_{\mathcal B}^+=x_{\mathcal B}-d\theta\), set \(x_q^+=\theta\) with all other nonbasic variables zero, and replace the basic index at position \(p\) by \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a primal-feasible basis of a standard-form minimization LP, solve the dual basis system and compute the nonbasic reduced costs. Stop at an optimum if all reduced costs are nonnegative. Otherwise choose a negative-reduced-cost entering variable and compute its basis direction. A componentwise nonpositive direction yields an unbounded ray. If the direction has a positive component, take the minimum-ratio step and exchange a limiting basic variable with the entering variable.
assumptions_latex: \min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}
B=A_{\mathcal B}\text{ is nonsingular}
x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b\geq0,\quad x_{\mathcal N}=0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The iteration returns an optimal point, detects an unbounded ray, or produces an updated primal-feasible basis by a minimum-ratio pivot.}

children.title: Dantzig Pricing
children.top_down_role: The classical largest reduced-cost-violation family.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has full row rank and \(B\) is a primal-feasible basis.
The linear program is maximized in standard form: \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An entering index is selected from \(\arg\max_{j\in N}\bar c_j\) whenever \(\max_{j\in N}\bar c_j>0\).

notation.meaning: reduced cost of nonbasic variable j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization-form primal simplex convention; ties may be resolved by any fixed rule.

source_refs.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given the reduced costs \(\bar c_j=c_j-c_B^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}A_j\) for all \(j\in N\), form the eligible set \(E=\{j\in N:\bar c_j>0\}\). If \(E=\varnothing\), pricing reports that no improving nonbasic variable exists. Otherwise Dantzig pricing chooses any \(q\in\arg\max_{j\in E}\bar c_j\). Thus the rule maximizes the instantaneous reduced-cost violation, without accounting for the feasible step length or the geometric length of the associated edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dantzig pricing enters an eligible nonbasic variable having the largest positive reduced cost; it reports no improving candidate when all reduced costs are nonpositive.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Eligible Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered primal-simplex pricing under the maximization reduced-cost convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Inspect \(j_1,j_2,\ldots,j_{|N|}\) sequentially. Stop at the first index \(j_k\) satisfying \(\bar c_{j_k}>0\), and return \(q=j_k\) as the entering index. If every index is inspected without satisfying the test, return that no improving candidate exists. The order is retained independently of the magnitudes of eligible reduced costs, so candidates following \(q\) are not evaluated during that pricing call.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan nonbasic variables in a fixed order and select the first with positive reduced cost; stop immediately once one is found.
assumptions_latex: The nonbasic indices have a fixed total order \(j_1\prec\cdots\prec j_{|N|}\).
Eligibility for maximization means \(\bar c_j>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected index is \(q=j_k\), where \(k=\min\{t:\bar c_{j_t}>0\}\), or no index if this set is empty.

knowledge_statements.title: Largest-Improvement Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-simplex largest-improvement pricing in standard form, including detection of an unbounded eligible direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every eligible nonbasic index \(j\in E=\{j\in N:\bar c_j>0\}\), compute \(u^j=B^{-1}A_j\). If some eligible \(j\) has \(u_i^j\le 0\) for every \(i\), that direction certifies primal unboundedness. Otherwise compute its blocking step \(\theta_j=\min_{i:u_i^j>0}(x_B)_i/u_i^j\) and predicted objective change \(\Delta_j=\bar c_j\theta_j\). Largest-improvement pricing selects any \(q\in\arg\max_{j\in E}\Delta_j\). If \(E=\varnothing\), it reports no improving candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each eligible variable, compute its reduced cost times its maximum feasible step and enter one giving the largest predicted objective improvement; an eligible direction without a blocking component signals unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a primal-feasible basis for a maximization problem in standard form.
The basic vector is \(x_B=B^{-1}b\ge 0\), and the nonbasic reduced costs are \(\bar c_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every eligible direction is blocked, choose \(q\in\arg\max_{j\in E}\bar c_j\theta_j\); if an eligible direction has no positive component, report primal unboundedness.

children.title: Primal Steepest-Edge Pricing
children.top_down_role: Normalized pricing in primal edge space.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a primal-feasible basis for \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\).
The problem uses the maximization reduced-cost convention \(\bar c_j>0\).

notation.meaning: full primal edge direction for increasing variable j

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(j\in E\), increasing \(x_j\) by one unit induces the full-space direction \(d^j\) with \(d^j_j=1\), \(d^j_B=-B^{-1}A_j\), and all other components zero. Its squared Euclidean length is \(\gamma_j=1+\|B^{-1}A_j\|_2^2\). Primal steepest-edge pricing selects any \(q\in\arg\max_{j\in E}\bar c_j/\sqrt{\gamma_j}\). If \(E=\varnothing\), it reports no improving entering variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the eligible entering variable with the greatest reduced-cost gain per unit Euclidean length of its primal edge direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal steepest-edge pricing and economical edge-weight updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-simplex entering-variable selection normalized by edge length; other pricing strategies in the extract are contextual and are not assigned to this narrower node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primal-feasible simplex basis \(B\) and nonbasic index set \(\mathcal N\), define \(\eta_i=[-B^{-1}A_i;e_i]\), \(s_i=c^T\eta_i\), and \(\gamma_i=\|\eta_i\|^2=\|B^{-1}A_i\|^2+1\). Primal steepest-edge pricing selects an improving index \(q\in\arg\min_{i\in\mathcal N,\,s_i<0}s_i/\sqrt{\gamma_i}\). If the entering column replaces basis position \(1\), let \(d=B^{-1}A_q\) and solve \(B^T\widehat d=d\) and \(B^Tr=e_1\). Then, for each old nonbasic index \(i\ne q\), \(\gamma_i^+=\gamma_i-2\frac{r^TA_i}{r^TA_q}\widehat d^TA_i+\left(\frac{r^TA_i}{r^TA_q}\right)^2\gamma_q\). Thus all relevant edge weights can be updated using two transposed-basis solves and column inner products. The rule does not guarantee that the selected edge admits a substantial feasible step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal steepest-edge pricing chooses the improving nonbasic variable with the most negative reduced objective change per unit edge length. After a pivot, all relevant squared edge lengths can be updated using two transposed-basis solves and column inner products. Favorable normalized descent still does not guarantee a long feasible step.
assumptions_latex: B\text{ is a nonsingular primal-feasible basis and }\mathcal N\text{ is its nonbasic index set}.
\eta_i=[-B^{-1}A_i;e_i],\quad s_i=c^T\eta_i,\quad \gamma_i=\|\eta_i\|^2.
\{i\in\mathcal N:s_i<0\}\ne\varnothing.
\text{For the displayed update, the entering column replaces basis position }1\text{ and }r^TA_q\ne0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q\in\arg\min_{i\in\mathcal N,\,s_i<0}\frac{s_i}{\sqrt{\gamma_i}},\qquad \gamma_i^+=\gamma_i-2\frac{r^TA_i}{r^TA_q}\widehat d^TA_i+\left(\frac{r^TA_i}{r^TA_q}\right)^2\gamma_q.

children.title: Dual Steepest-Edge Pricing
children.top_down_role: Normalized pricing in dual edge space.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is dual feasible in a dual-simplex iteration.
The leaving candidates are rows \(i\) whose basic values violate primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Select a leaving row maximizing normalized primal infeasibility, \(p\in\arg\max_{i\in I}|(x_B)_i|/\sqrt{w_i}\).

notation.meaning: squared Euclidean norm of the associated dual edge covector

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard dual-simplex leaving-row interpretation; the immutable path creates a role ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=\{i:(x_B)_i<0\}\) be the primal-infeasible basic rows under the usual lower-bound convention. Associate with row \(i\) the dual-space edge covector \(e_i^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}\) and weight \(w_i=\|e_i^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}\|_2^2\). Dual steepest-edge pricing selects any \(p\in\arg\max_{i\in I}|(x_B)_i|/\sqrt{w_i}\); the subsequent dual ratio test chooses the entering column. If \(I=\varnothing\), primal feasibility has been restored.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In dual simplex, select the infeasible leaving row with the largest primal violation normalized by its dual-edge length.

assumptions_latex: Each eligible pivot candidate \(j\) has an improving directional derivative \(g_j>0\).
A positive-definite metric \(H\) is fixed on the chosen representation space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metric steepest-edge variant selects \(q\in\arg\max_{j\in E}g_j/\sqrt{(v^j)^{\mathsf T}Hv^j}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent each eligible pivot direction by a vector \(v^j\) in a chosen variable or transformed space and equip that space with the norm \(\|v\|_H=\sqrt{v^{\mathsf T}Hv}\), where \(H\succ0\). The corresponding steepest-edge score is \(g_j/\|v^j\|_H\), and the rule chooses any maximizing candidate. Different variants result from representing \(v^j\) in the full primal-variable space, the basic-variable space, or a dual/transformed space; they coincide only when their induced directional norms agree.

children.title: Devex Weight Models
children.top_down_role: Approximate edge-length representations used by Devex pricing.

assumptions_latex: The current iteration has eligible candidates \(E\) with reduced costs \(\bar c_j>0\).
Every maintained Devex weight satisfies \(w_j>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Devex selects \(q\in\arg\max_{j\in E}\bar c_j/\sqrt{w_j}\), with \(w_j\) approximating an exact squared edge norm.

notation.meaning: exact squared edge length being approximated

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract Devex weight model, excluding implementation-specific recurrence formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Devex model maintains positive scalars \(w_j\) intended to approximate the exact squared edge lengths \(\gamma_j\) used by steepest-edge pricing. At a pricing call it assigns candidate \(j\) the normalized score \(s_j=\bar c_j/\sqrt{w_j}\) and chooses any \(q\in\arg\max_{j\in E}s_j\). After a pivot, the weights are updated from inexpensive tableau information rather than recomputing every \(\gamma_j\). Positivity of all \(w_j\) is required for the scores to remain defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Devex stores positive approximate squared edge lengths and prices candidates by reduced cost divided by the square root of the stored weight.
knowledge_statements.title: Devex Weight Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and normalized score are plausible for Devex, but no source is provided for the interpretation of maintained weights as approximate squared edge lengths or for their tableau-based updating.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reference-framework edge weights and their inexpensive approximate update in primal-simplex pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primal-feasible simplex basis, steepest-edge pricing selects an eligible \(\beta\) maximizing \(r_\beta/\sqrt{T_\beta}\), where \(T_j=1+\sum_{i=1}^m q_{ij}^2\). Devex measures edge length only in a reference framework and maintains approximations \(\widetilde T_j\), initialized to \(1\) when the current nonbasic variables form that framework. After a pivot with leaving row \(\alpha\) and entering column \(\beta\), it sets \(\widetilde T_j^+=\max\{\widetilde T_j,(q_{\alpha j}/q_{\alpha\beta})^2\widetilde T_\beta\}\). Because these approximations grow and can deteriorate, the reference framework and all weights are periodically reset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Devex approximates steepest-edge normalization using weights measured in a reference set of variables. It initializes the weights to one, applies a maximum-based update after each pivot, and periodically resets them when the approximations deteriorate.
assumptions_latex: x_B=p+Qx_N,\quad z=z_0+r^Tx_N
B\text{ is primal feasible}
r_\beta>0,\quad q_{\alpha\beta}\ne0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widetilde T_j^+=\max\!\left\{\widetilde T_j,\left(\frac{q_{\alpha j}}{q_{\alpha\beta}}\right)^2\widetilde T_\beta\right\}\text{ is the Devex surrogate-weight update.}

children.title: Devex Reinitialization Regimes
children.top_down_role: Restart and reset policies for accumulated pricing information.

assumptions_latex: A Devex implementation maintains positive weights \(w_j\) and can compute reference weights \(w_j^{\mathrm{ref}}>0\).
A specified reliability predicate \(R(w,w^{\mathrm{ref}})\) is evaluated after pivots.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever \(R(w,w^{\mathrm{ref}})\) fails, replace \(w_j\) by \(w_j^{\mathrm{ref}}\) for all active candidates before subsequent pricing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic reset regime; numerical thresholds and reference-weight formulas are implementation dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the active weights by \(w_j=w_j^{\mathrm{ref}}>0\). After each pivot, apply the chosen Devex recurrence and evaluate a prescribed reliability predicate \(R(w,w^{\mathrm{ref}})\). A regime may trigger periodically, after numerical instability, or when approximate and reference scales differ beyond a specified threshold. On a trigger, discard accumulated weights, set \(w_j\leftarrow w_j^{\mathrm{ref}}\) for every active candidate, and restart accumulation. Between triggers, retain and update the current weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reset all accumulated Devex weights to fresh positive reference values whenever a prescribed periodic or reliability trigger fires.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition or cover \(N\) by ordered blocks \(N_1,\ldots,N_r\). Starting from a designated block, evaluate only that block and form \(E_k\). If \(E_k\ne\varnothing\), return an accepted candidate, commonly a maximizer of \(s_j\) over \(E_k\), without scanning the remaining blocks. Otherwise advance to the next block. A conclusion that no eligible candidate exists is valid only after all blocks have been examined without an intervening basis change.

children.title: Multiple Pricing
children.top_down_role: Retention of several candidates across nearby pivots.

assumptions_latex: A full or partial scan produces a finite pool \(P\) of eligible candidates.
Pool entries can be retested after each basis change.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Retain several candidates, pivot using the current best valid member, and rescan when the retained pool becomes empty or unreliable.

notation.meaning: current valid members of the pool

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic retained-pool multiple pricing; refresh and pool-size policies remain unspecified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: During a pricing scan, retain a pool \(P\) containing several eligible candidates, typically those with the largest scores. Choose a pivot candidate from \(P\). After the pivot, update or recompute the eligibility and score of each retained index, discard invalid members, and choose the next pivot from \(P^{\mathrm{valid}}\) without an immediate global rescan. Perform a new full or partial scan when \(P^{\mathrm{valid}}=\varnothing\) or when a prescribed reliability condition requires refreshing the pool.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keep several promising candidates from one scan, reuse valid members over nearby pivots, and refresh the pool when it is exhausted or unreliable.

children.title: Ordinary Minimum-Ratio Test
children.top_down_role: The canonical primal blocking-test family.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is primal feasible with basic vector \(x_B=B^{-1}b\ge0\).
An eligible entering index \(q\) has direction \(u=B^{-1}A_q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If some \(u_i>0\), the maximum feasible step is \(\theta^*=\min_{i:u_i>0}(x_B)_i/u_i\), and any minimizing row may leave.

notation.meaning: basic-variable change per unit increase of the entering variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form primal simplex with nonnegative variables and an ordinary blocking test.

source_refs.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For step \(\theta\ge0\) in entering variable \(q\), the basic variables become \(x_B(\theta)=x_B-\theta u\), where \(u=B^{-1}A_q\). If \(u_i\le0\) for every \(i\), no basic variable blocks the step and an improving entering direction is unbounded. Otherwise set \(\theta^*=\min_{i:u_i>0}(x_B)_i/u_i\). Any row attaining this minimum is eligible to leave; at \(\theta^*\), primal feasibility is preserved and at least one blocking basic variable reaches zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increase the entering variable until the first basic variable reaches zero; a minimizing blocking row leaves, while no positive direction component signals unboundedness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes tied blockers in the primal simplex ratio test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a primal-feasible basis have basic vector \(x_B\ge 0\), and let an entering variable increase with basic direction \(x_B(t)=x_B-t d\). Define \(I_+=\{i:d_i>0\}\) and \(\theta^*=\min_{i\in I_+}x_{B_i}/d_i\). The tie set is \(T=\{i\in I_+:x_{B_i}/d_i=\theta^*\}\). If \(|T|>1\), every \(i\in T\) is an admissible leaving index and all tied components reach zero at \(t=\theta^*\). Choosing one tied index leaves the others basic at zero, so the resulting basis is degenerate and subsequent pivot behavior may depend on the tie-breaking rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Several rows may attain the same minimum ratio. Any may leave, while the other tied basic variables remain zero and create degeneracy-sensitive pivot choices.
assumptions_latex: \(x_B\ge 0\) is a primal-feasible basic solution.
\(I_+\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|T|>1\Rightarrow x_{B_i}(\theta^*)=0\) for every \(i\in T\), with each \(i\in T\) an admissible leaving index.

notation.meaning: Basic-variable decrease direction induced by the entering variable.
Set of rows attaining the minimum ratio.

children.title: Harris Feasibility Window
children.top_down_role: Tolerance-band organization of admissible blockers.

knowledge_statements.title: Harris Feasibility Window
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the relaxed primal blocking interval used by Harris selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primal-feasible basic vector \(x_B\), direction \(x_B(t)=x_B-t d\), and feasibility tolerance \(\varepsilon_f\ge 0\), define the Harris step limit by \(\bar\theta_H=\min_{i:d_i>0}(x_{B_i}+\varepsilon_f)/d_i\), with \(\bar\theta_H=+\infty\) if no \(d_i>0\). The Harris feasibility window is \(W_H=\{t:0\le t\le\bar\theta_H\}\). Every \(t\in W_H\) satisfies \(x_{B_i}(t)\ge-\varepsilon_f\) for all \(i\); a row is an admissible second-pass blocker when \(d_i>0\) and its exact breakpoint \(x_{B_i}/d_i\) does not exceed \(\bar\theta_H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Harris enlarges the exact feasible interval by a tolerance, then admits every positive-direction row whose exact breakpoint lies inside that relaxed window.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon_f\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t\in W_H\Rightarrow x_B-t d\ge-\varepsilon_f\mathbf 1.
review_flags: Exact Harris convention and authoritative locator require confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a plausible Harris feasibility-window convention, but no inspectable source establishes the precise tolerance and second-pass eligibility convention.

children.title: Harris Two-Pass Selection
children.top_down_role: The two-stage Harris pivot-selection family.

knowledge_statements.title: Harris Two-Pass Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal two-pass Harris rule with maximum-pivot second-pass selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(x_B\ge0\), direction \(d\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon_f\ge0\). First compute \(\bar\theta_H=\min_{i:d_i>0}(x_{B_i}+\varepsilon_f)/d_i\). If no \(d_i>0\), report no blocker. Otherwise form \(C_H=\{i:d_i>0,\ x_{B_i}/d_i\le\bar\theta_H\}\). In the second pass choose \(p\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{i\in C_H}|d_i|\), with a deterministic rule for residual ties, and pivot on row \(p\). The accepted step is \(\theta=x_{B_p}/d_p\); hence \(\theta\le\bar\theta_H\), while maximizing \(|d_p|\) discourages numerically small pivot elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First compute a tolerance-relaxed step limit; then, among exact blockers inside that limit, choose a row having the largest pivot magnitude.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon_f\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_H\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow p\in C_H\text{ and }0\le\theta=x_{B_p}/d_p\le\bar\theta_H.
review_flags: Exact Harris convention and authoritative locator require confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated two-pass rule is plausible, but Harris implementations differ in their relaxed ratios, candidate sets, and accepted step. An authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Ordinary Dual Ratio Test
children.top_down_role: The canonical dual-feasibility blocking-test family.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Dual Ratio Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-simplex ratio test for a minimization problem in equality form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), with basis index set \(\mathcal B\), nonsingular basis matrix \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\), and nonbasic index set \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal B\). Suppose the basis is dual feasible, so \(r_j=c_j-a_j^TB^{-T}c_{\mathcal B}\ge0\) for every \(j\in N\), and choose a basis position \(p\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with \((B^{-1}b)_p<0\). Define \(\alpha_j=(B^{-1}a_j)_p\) and \(C=\{j\in N:\alpha_j<0\}\). If \(C\ne\varnothing\), choose \(q\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{j\in C}r_j/(-\alpha_j)\), using deterministic tie-breaking, and pivot in position \((p,q)\). The dual step \(\theta=r_q/(-\alpha_q)\) preserves nonnegativity of the updated reduced costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a negative basic row of a dual-feasible basis, choose an eligible nonbasic column minimizing its reduced cost divided by the negative tableau-row coefficient; the resulting pivot preserves dual feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) is nonsingular.
\(r_j\ge0\) for every \(j\in N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow q\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{j\in C}\frac{r_j}{-\alpha_j}\text{ and the pivot preserves dual feasibility}.

notation.meaning: Reduced cost of nonbasic variable j.
Coefficient of column j in the selected tableau row.

children.title: Dual Harris Ratio Test
children.top_down_role: The dual-simplex specialization of tolerance-aware Harris control.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Harris Ratio Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-aware two-pass ratio selection for the dual simplex method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a dual-simplex leaving row \(p\), let \(r_j\ge0\) be nonbasic reduced costs, \(\alpha_j=(B^{-1}a_j)_p\), and \(C=\{j:\alpha_j<0\}\). Given dual tolerance \(\varepsilon_d\ge0\), first compute \(\bar\theta_H=\min_{j\in C}(r_j+\varepsilon_d)/(-\alpha_j)\). Then form \(C_H=\{j\in C:r_j/(-\alpha_j)\le\bar\theta_H\}\) and choose \(q\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{j\in C_H}|\alpha_j|\), resolving residual ties deterministically. Pivot on \((p,q)\). If \(C\) is empty, report no dual blocker rather than pivoting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual Harris test builds a tolerance-relaxed ratio window and selects a numerically large tableau coefficient among the exact ratios inside it.
assumptions_latex: The current basis is dual feasible.
\(x_{B_p}<0\) and \(\varepsilon_d\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow q\in C_H\text{ and }\frac{r_q}{-\alpha_q}\le\bar\theta_H.

children.title: Opposite-Bound Events
children.top_down_role: Steps ending at the alternate bound without an ordinary leaving-variable exchange.

knowledge_statements.title: Opposite-Bound Events
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a bounded nonbasic variable reaching its alternate bound during a step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a bounded variable satisfy \(\ell_j\le x_j\le u_j\) with \(\ell_j<u_j<+\infty\), and suppose it starts nonbasic at one bound. Along \(x_j(t)=x_j(0)+t d_j\), an opposite-bound event occurs at a finite \(\tau_j>0\) when \(x_j(\tau_j)\) equals the other bound and \(x_j(t)\) remains within \([\ell_j,u_j]\) for \(0\le t\le\tau_j\). At the event, the variable's nonbasic status changes from lower-bound to upper-bound status or conversely; no basic variable need leave, so the basis matrix can remain unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonbasic bounded variable traverses its interval and reaches the other bound; its bound status flips without requiring a basis exchange.
assumptions_latex: \(-\infty<\ell_j<u_j<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_j(\tau_j)\in\{\ell_j,u_j\}\setminus\{x_j(0)\}\text{ and the basis may remain unchanged}.

notation.meaning: Time at which the alternate bound is reached.
Step direction of the bounded variable.

children.title: Bound-Flipping Ratio Tests
children.top_down_role: Long-step dual control through intervening bound changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Flipping Ratio Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Long-step bounded-variable dual control through intermediate bound flips.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a dual-simplex leaving row, bounded nonbasic variables, and their nonnegative ordered breakpoint ratios \(0\le\tau_1\le\cdots\le\tau_m\). Traverse the breakpoints in order while maintaining the cumulative primal correction and the reduced-cost feasibility interval. At breakpoint \(\tau_k\), if the associated variable can move from its current bound to its opposite bound without violating dual feasibility, flip its bound status and update the cumulative correction without changing the basis. Stop at the first breakpoint admitting the required entering-variable pivot; perform that pivot and output the accumulated flips together with the new basis. Report no blocker if no breakpoint admits a pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A long-step dual test crosses ordered breakpoints, flips eligible nonbasic variables to opposite bounds, and pivots only at the first required basis exchange.
assumptions_latex: All participating variables have finite stated bounds.
Breakpoints are computed for a fixed dual-search direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output consists of zero or more feasibility-preserving bound flips followed by at most one basis pivot.

notation.meaning: The kth ordered breakpoint along the dual step.

review_flags: Algorithm variants differ in cumulative slope and admissibility tests; a precise authoritative source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Bound-flipping ratio tests use implementation-specific slope updates and admissibility tests. The supplied generic description cannot be validated without a precise authoritative algorithm.

children.title: Multiple-Breakpoint Control

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Breakpoint Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic event-ordered control for a piecewise-linear bounded-variable step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z(t)=z^0+t d\) be a search path and let each bounded component contribute every positive time at which it reaches a bound. Sort the distinct event times as \(0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_s\). Starting at \(t=0\), advance successively to \(\tau_k\), process all components tied at that time as one event set, update their bound statuses and the active affine segment, and recompute or validate later breakpoints. Stop when a basis-exchange condition, feasibility limit, or prescribed terminal step is reached. Event ties must be processed atomically or by a deterministic rule that gives the same admissible post-event state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order all bound breakpoints, process simultaneous events together, update the active path after each event, and stop at the first terminal or pivot condition.
assumptions_latex: Each component has fixed finite or infinite bounds.
The path is affine between consecutive processed events.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The controlled step is partitioned into finitely many affine segments separated by ordered breakpoint event sets.
review_flags: A bounded-variable simplex locator is needed to certify the intended breakpoint-update convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The event-ordered algorithm fits the leaf, but its atomic tie processing and breakpoint recomputation requirements need a bounded-variable simplex source.

children.title: Primal No-Blocker Regime
children.top_down_role: The primal ratio-test boundary associated with an improving unbounded direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal No-Blocker Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unboundedness certificate produced by a blocker-free primal ratio test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and let \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) be a nonsingular basis matrix with basic feasible solution \(x\) defined by \(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b\ge0\) and \(x_N=0\). Let \(q\in N\) have reduced cost \(r_q=c_q-c_{\mathcal B}^TB^{-1}a_q<0\), and put \(d=B^{-1}a_q\). If \(d\le0\), define \(h_q=1\), \(h_{\mathcal B}=-d\), and \(h_j=0\) for \(j\in N\setminus\{q\}\). Then \(h\ge0\), \(Ah=0\), and \(c^Th=r_q<0\). Consequently \(x+th\) is feasible for every \(t\ge0\) and its objective tends to \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an improving entering column causes no basic variable to decrease, the current basic feasible solution and its tableau direction define a feasible ray with strictly decreasing objective, certifying unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) is nonsingular.
\(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b\ge0\) and \(x_N=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\ge0,\quad Ah=0,\quad c^Th<0,\quad\text{so the primal problem is unbounded below}.

notation.meaning: Reduced cost of the entering variable.

children.title: Dual No-Blocker Regime
children.top_down_role: The dual ratio-test boundary associated with primal infeasibility certification.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual No-Blocker Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas infeasibility certificate produced by a blocker-free dual ratio test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), consider \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\). Let \(\mathcal B\) be a basis index set, let \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) be nonsingular, and choose a basis-row position \(p\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) such that \((B^{-1}b)_p<0\). Set \(w=B^{-T}e_p\). If \((B^{-1}a_j)_p\ge0\) for every nonbasic index \(j\in N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal B\), then \(A^Tw\ge0\): the basic-column components equal \(B^Tw=e_p\ge0\), and the nonbasic-column components equal the stated row coefficients. Moreover \(b^Tw=(B^{-1}b)_p<0\). Hence \(w\) is a Farkas certificate that \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\) is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a negative basic row has no eligible nonbasic entering column, its basis-row multiplier is nonnegative on every column and negative on the right-hand side, providing a Farkas certificate of primal infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) is nonsingular.
\((B^{-1}a_j)_p\ge0\) for every \(j\in N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^Tw\ge0\text{ and }b^Tw<0,\quad\text{so }\{x\ge0:Ax=b\}=\varnothing.

notation.meaning: The pth coordinate vector in the ordered basis-row space.

children.title: Single-Exchange Pivot Control

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Exchange Pivot Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical simplex update with one entering and one leaving index.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an ordered basis index set \(\mathcal B=(b_1,\ldots,b_m)\) with nonsingular basis matrix \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\), a nonbasic entering index \(q\), and an admissible leaving position \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Let \(p=b_i\) be the leaving column index and suppose the pivot element \((B^{-1}a_q)_i\ne0\). Replace exactly one index by setting \(\mathcal B'=(\mathcal B\setminus\{p\})\cup\{q\}\), preserving the inherited ordering with \(q\) in position \(i\). Update the basic solution and reduced costs using \(A_{\mathcal B'}\), and accept the exchange only when the selected primal or dual ratio test guarantees the required feasibility invariant. Each accepted iteration changes the basis by one entering-leaving exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-exchange pivot replaces one basic column by one nonbasic column at a nonzero pivot position and preserves the feasibility invariant enforced by the applicable ratio test.
assumptions_latex: \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) is nonsingular.
\(q\notin\mathcal B\), \(p=b_i\in\mathcal B\), and \((B^{-1}a_q)_i\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\mathcal B\setminus\mathcal B'|=|\mathcal B'\setminus\mathcal B|=1\text{ and }A_{\mathcal B'}\text{ is nonsingular}.

notation.meaning: Leaving position in the ordered basis.

children.title: Block Pivoting
children.top_down_role: Grouped basis exchanges and their admissibility regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Pivoting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous exchange of equally sized entering and leaving index blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an ordered basis index set \(\mathcal B=(b_1,\ldots,b_m)\) with nonsingular basis matrix \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\). Choose a set of leaving positions \(R=\{i_1,\ldots,i_k\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and an ordered set of distinct entering indices \(E=(e_1,\ldots,e_k)\subseteq N\), where \(k\ge2\). Let \(L=\{b_i:i\in R\}\) and form the block pivot matrix \(M=(B^{-1}A_E)_{R,:}\in\mathbb R^{k\times k}\), using the stated orders of \(R\) and \(E\). If \(M\) is nonsingular, replace the columns indexed by \(L\) with those indexed by \(E\) in the corresponding positions, obtaining \(\mathcal B'=(\mathcal B\setminus L)\cup E\). Compute the new basic solution and reduced costs and accept the grouped exchange only if the required primal or dual feasibility conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block pivoting replaces equally many specified basis positions and nonbasic columns at once. A nonsingular block pivot matrix yields a nonsingular candidate basis, which is accepted only when the required feasibility conditions hold.
assumptions_latex: \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) is nonsingular.
\(R\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), \(E\subseteq N\), and \(|R|=|E|=k\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ nonsingular}\Rightarrow A_{\mathcal B'}\text{ nonsingular and }|\mathcal B'|=|\mathcal B|=m.

notation.meaning: Ordered set of leaving positions in the basis.
Basic column indices occupying the leaving positions.
Ordered block of entering nonbasic column indices.

children.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Tolerance systems governing primal and dual eligibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute primal and dual feasibility tests for a standard-form minimization basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\). For a basis \(B\), set \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\), \(y=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\), and \(r_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}y\). Given \(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d\ge0\), the basis is numerically primal feasible when \(x_{B,i}\ge-\varepsilon_p\) for every \(i\in B\) and numerically dual feasible when \(r_j\ge-\varepsilon_d\) for every \(j\in N\). A nonbasic index is primal-simplex entering-eligible only if \(r_j<-\varepsilon_d\); a basic index is dual-simplex leaving-eligible only if \(x_{B,i}<-\varepsilon_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate primal and dual tolerances determine whether basic values, reduced costs, and their corresponding pivot candidates count as feasible or violating.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
\(A_B\) is nonsingular.
The problem uses the stated minimization and reduced-cost convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_B\ge-\varepsilon_p\mathbf1\) and \(r_N\ge-\varepsilon_d\mathbf1\) are the respective numerical feasibility predicates.

children.title: Pivot-Magnitude Screening
children.top_down_role: Numerical-quality screening among otherwise admissible pivots.

knowledge_statements.title: Pivot-Magnitude Screening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A relative screen for rejecting numerically small primal-simplex pivot elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an entering-eligible index \(j\), compute \(u=A_B^{-1}a_j\). A ratio-test candidate \(i\in B\) with \(u_i>0\) passes relative pivot-magnitude screening at threshold \(\tau\in(0,1]\) precisely when \(|u_i|\ge\tau\lVert u\rVert_\infty\). The leaving index must be selected only among passing candidates, using the prescribed feasibility ratio rule. If no candidate passes, the pivot is rejected by this screen; that rejection alone is not a certificate of primal unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An admissible leaving candidate is retained only when its pivot component is not too small relative to the transformed entering column.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular.
The entering index has already passed reduced-cost eligibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted candidate set is \(\{i\in B:u_i>0,\ |u_i|\ge\tau\lVert u\rVert_\infty\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relative pivot screen is coherent and correctly avoids treating rejection as an unboundedness certificate, but the exact infinity-norm scaling rule and threshold policy are solver-specific and have no cited source.

children.title: Post-Pivot Discrepancy Cleanup
children.top_down_role: Solver controls for small bound and feasibility discrepancies after pivot selection.

children.title: Bound-Discrepancy Cleanup
children.top_down_role: Controls for small post-selection discrepancies relative to variable bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Discrepancy Cleanup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-preserving cleanup for nonbasic variables lying numerically near their assigned bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\) with \(l\le x\le u\), let each nonbasic index \(j\in N\) have an assigned finite bound \(\bar x_j\in\{l_j,u_j\}\). Given \(\varepsilon_b\ge0\), replace \(x_j\) by \(\bar x_j\) whenever \(|x_j-\bar x_j|\le\varepsilon_b\); otherwise report unresolved bound discrepancy. After all replacements, recompute \(x_B=A_B^{-1}(b-A_Nx_N)\). Output the cleaned vector only if it satisfies the chosen joint feasibility tests; otherwise retain the original iterate and report cleanup failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Snap near-bound nonbasic values to their assigned bounds, recompute the basic variables, and accept only if all feasibility checks still pass.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular.
Every cleaned nonbasic variable has a finite assigned bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted output has \(x_N=\bar x_N\) on cleaned indices and satisfies \(Ax=b\) up to the linear-solve accuracy.

notation.meaning: Assigned lower or upper bounds of nonbasic variables.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the cleanup leaf, but snapping, recomputation, rollback, and joint-acceptance behavior constitute a particular implementation policy unsupported by evidence.

children.title: Feasibility-Discrepancy Cleanup
children.top_down_role: Controls for small post-selection primal or dual feasibility discrepancies.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Discrepancy Cleanup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual correction with a fixed basis followed by joint feasibility validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a bounded LP iterate \(x\) and nonsingular basis matrix \(A_B\), compute the equality residual \(q=b-Ax\). Solve \(A_Bd_B=q\), set \(x_B\leftarrow x_B+d_B\), and leave \(x_N\) fixed. Repeat until \(\lVert b-Ax\rVert\le\varepsilon_f\) or a prescribed refinement limit is reached. Output the corrected iterate only if \(l-\varepsilon_b\mathbf1\le x\le u+\varepsilon_b\mathbf1\); otherwise report that residual cleanup conflicts with bound feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Correct equality residuals through the current basis while holding nonbasic values fixed, then reject any correction that creates an excessive bound violation.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular.
The residual norm and refinement limit are fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful cleanup yields \(\lVert b-Ax\rVert\le\varepsilon_f\) without violating the bound tolerance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The basis correction equation is mathematically coherent, but the iterative-refinement stopping rule, correction policy, and acceptance behavior require an implementation or numerical-linear-algebra source.

children.title: Cleanup Interaction Boundary
children.top_down_role: Cases where correcting one discrepancy can affect the status of another.

knowledge_statements.title: Cleanup Interaction Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint acceptance boundary for bound snapping and equality-residual correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Bound cleanup and feasibility cleanup are not independently safe. If snapping produces \(\Delta x_N\), preserving \(Ax=b\) requires \(\Delta x_B=-A_B^{-1}A_N\Delta x_N\), which may violate a basic bound. Conversely, a residual correction \(d_B=A_B^{-1}(b-Ax)\) may move a basic component outside its tolerance interval. Therefore cleanup is admissible only when the final vector simultaneously satisfies the equality-residual test and every bound-feasibility test; otherwise the combined cleanup must fail or trigger a basis change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Snapping nonbasic values and correcting equality residuals can create new basic-bound violations, so cleanup is accepted only after a joint final check.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Stalling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite primal-simplex stalling caused by consecutive degenerate pivots.

Stalling alone does not assert recurrence: the bases \(B_k,\ldots,B_{k+r}\) may all be distinct or some may recur.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Lexicographic Pivoting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal lexicographic minimum-ratio test using fixed ordered perturbation components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_B\) be the current basis matrix, let \(\beta=A_B^{-1}b\), and let \(u=A_B^{-1}A_e\) be the basic direction for an improving entering column \(A_e\). For every blocking row \(i\) with \(u_i>0\), let \(h_i^T\) be row \(i\) of \(A_B^{-1}\) and form \(v_i=u_i^{-1}(\beta_i,h_i^T)\), with the components of \(h_i\) written in the fixed perturbation order. Choose the row whose \(v_i\) is lexicographically smallest and pivot. Distinct blocking rows cannot have identical normalized perturbation rows because the rows of \(A_B^{-1}\) are linearly independent, so the leaving row is unique. Repeating this rule preserves lexicographic feasibility and prevents recurrence; because only finitely many bases exist, the primal-simplex run terminates at an optimal basis or an unboundedness certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each blocking row, divide its basic value and ordered inverse-basis perturbation row by the positive entering-direction component, then choose the lexicographically smallest vector. This uniquely resolves blocking ties and prevents primal-simplex cycling.
assumptions_latex: The linear program is in standard form, the current dictionary is primal feasible, and an improving nonbasic column \(A_e\) has been selected to enter.
The basis matrix \(A_B\) is nonsingular, a fixed order is imposed on the right-hand-side perturbation components, and the current augmented basic-value rows are lexicographically feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lexicographic ratio rule selects a unique leaving row, preserves lexicographic feasibility, and excludes recurrence of a primal-simplex basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Finiteness-to-Complexity Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical separation between anti-cycling termination and efficient pivot complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal B\) be the finite set of admissible bases and suppose a deterministic pivot rule never revisits a basis. Then every run has fewer than \(|\mathcal B|\) pivots. This establishes finite termination, but the estimate is generally exponential because \(|\mathcal B|\le {n\choose m}\). A polynomial complexity conclusion requires an additional argument bounding the visited subset or another computational resource by a polynomial in the input encoding length. Therefore finiteness of the state space and acyclicity of the pivot trajectory alone do not establish polynomial-time solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acyclic motion on finitely many bases proves termination, but polynomial complexity needs a separate polynomial bound on visited states or computational work.

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Finite Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-theoretic criterion for a deterministic simplex rule to be finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed linear program, form the directed basis graph \(G_R=(\mathcal B,E_R)\) of a deterministic pivot rule \(R\): its vertices are admissible bases, and \((B,B')\in E_R\) when \(R\) pivots from the nonterminal basis \(B\) to the adjacent basis \(B'\). The rule is finite from every admissible starting basis exactly when the reachable part of \(G_R\) contains no directed cycle. Equivalently, there exists a ranking \(\rho:\mathcal B\to\{0,\ldots,|\mathcal B|-1\}\) that strictly increases along every reachable rule edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic combinatorial pivot rule is finite exactly when its directed transitions among reachable bases are acyclic, equivalently when they admit a strict finite ranking.
assumptions_latex: The set \(\mathcal B\) of admissible bases is finite.
The rule selects at most one successor for each nonterminal basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R\text{ is finite}\iff G_R\text{ is acyclic on every reachable component}.

notation.meaning: directed basis-transition graph induced by rule R

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite directed-graph criterion is mathematically plausible, but no source connects this generic criterion to the surveyed class called “Combinatorial Finite Rules.” A specific source and locator are required.

children.title: Recursive Finite Rules

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Finite Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inductive construction of finite pivot rules on ordered faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_d\) be a deterministic pivot rule on every ordered polyhedral face of dimension at most \(d\). Suppose each invocation in dimension \(d>0\) either makes a pivot that strictly increases a finite outer rank \(q_d\), or restricts the problem to a proper face and invokes \(R_{d-1}\); after return, the same lower-dimensional subproblem is not invoked again at the same outer rank. If \(R_0\) terminates, then every \(R_d\) terminates. Indeed, an execution has finitely many outer-rank increases and, between them, finitely many terminating calls of smaller dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recursive pivot rule is finite when every step increases a finite rank or descends to a smaller face without repeating the same subproblem.
assumptions_latex: Every recursive call strictly lowers face dimension.
Each outer rank has a finite ordered range.
Equal-rank lower-dimensional subproblems are not repeated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_0\text{ finite}\Longrightarrow R_d\text{ finite for every finite }d\).

notation.meaning: rule restricted to faces of dimension at most d
finite outer ranking at recursion level d

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract induction principle is plausible, but it is not tied to an identified recursive simplex rule family. Its no-repeat and finite-rank hypotheses require a source showing that the intended surveyed rules satisfy them.

children.title: Ordering-to-Recursion Interface

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering-to-Recursion Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a finite ordered state space into recursive pivot control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((S_d,\prec_d)\) be the finite ordered state set at recursion level \(d\), and let \(T_d\) be its pivot transition map. Represent a state by \((r,s)\), where \(r\) is its outer-order rank and \(s\in S_{d-1}\) describes the active proper face. Require every transition either to replace \(r\) by a larger rank, or to keep \(r\) fixed and advance \(s\) according to the finite rule at level \(d-1\). Then lexicographic order on \((r,\rho_{d-1}(s))\) is a strict ranking for \(T_d\), connecting the combinatorial ordering with recursive finiteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An outer state order and a lower-dimensional rank combine lexicographically, turning recursive pivot transitions into strict progress on a finite ordered set.
assumptions_latex: Each \(S_d\) is finite and totally ordered.
The lower-level rank \(\rho_{d-1}\) strictly increases on recursive transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_d(r,s)\ne(r,s)\Longrightarrow (r,\rho_{d-1}(s))<_{\mathrm{lex}}(r',\rho_{d-1}(s'))\).

notation.meaning: finite state set at recursion level d

knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Finite Pivot Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite basis tracing along a generic one-parameter simplex path.

Decrease \(t\) until the first parameter value at which primal or dual feasibility becomes tight, pivot to the adjacent basis selected by the limiting ratio test, and continue. Stop at \(t=0\); return a basis whose limiting primal-dual solution is feasible and optimal for the unperturbed problem. Finiteness follows when breakpoints are distinct and no basis interval is revisited.

An optimal basis is known at \(t_0>0\).

children.title: EXPAND Anti-Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.title: EXPAND Anti-Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-expansion family for encouraging positive simplex steps in floating-point computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an initial feasibility tolerance \(\tau_0>0\), increment \(\delta>0\), maximum tolerance \(\tau_{\max}\), and reset period \(K\). At pivot \(k\), use \(\tau_k=\min\{\tau_0+(k\bmod K)\delta,\tau_{\max}\}\) in the ratio test, permitting controlled bound violations within \(\tau_k\). Among admissible leaving variables, select one supporting a step of at least a prescribed positive threshold whenever possible. After each block of \(K\) pivots, restore \(\tau_0\), recompute feasibility, and correct or reject iterates whose bound violations exceed the restored tolerance. Stop under the solver’s ordinary optimality or infeasibility tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: EXPAND gradually relaxes feasibility tolerance to encourage nonzero pivots, periodically resets it, and checks that accumulated bound violations remain controlled.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\tau_0\le\tau_{\max}\) and \(\delta>0\).
Feasibility is recomputed at each reset.
The implementation specifies a positive-step selection rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_0\le\tau_k\le\tau_{\max}\), with periodic restoration and feasibility correction.

children.title: Simplex Stall Detection

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Stall Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Windowed numerical predicate for declaring insufficient simplex progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given objective values \(z_k\), accepted step lengths \(\alpha_k\), a window \(W\ge1\), and tolerances \(\varepsilon_z,\varepsilon_\alpha>0\), declare a stall at iteration \(k\ge W\) when \[\max_{k-W<i\le k}\frac{|z_i-z_{i-1}|}{1+|z_{i-1}|}\le\varepsilon_z\] and either \[\max_{k-W<i\le k}\alpha_i\le\varepsilon_\alpha\] or every pivot in the window is classified as degenerate. The declaration is a policy trigger, not a certificate of optimality, infeasibility, cycling, or exact nonprogress.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stall is flagged when scaled objective change stays small over a window and all recent steps are tiny or classified as degenerate.
assumptions_latex: Accepted iterates supply \(z_i\) and \(\alpha_i\).
\(W\), \(\varepsilon_z\), and \(\varepsilon_\alpha\) are fixed before evaluating the window.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{stall}(k)=1\) exactly when the displayed windowed predicate holds.

knowledge_statements.title: EXPAND Cycling Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance expansion alone supplies no discrete descent invariant for the basis sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an EXPAND-type ratio test whose feasibility tolerance is \(\Delta_k=\Delta_0+k\delta\), with \(\delta>0\), and which permits a minimum signed step compatible with that tolerance. Increasing \(\Delta_k\) does not by itself impose a strict ordering on successive bases. Therefore finiteness cannot be inferred solely from \(\Delta_{k+1}>\Delta_k\): a termination claim additionally requires a proved nonrepetition rule, lexicographic descent, or another well-founded invariant. Cycling regimes remain logically admissible whenever accepted tolerance-level pivots can revisit a previous basis without decreasing such an invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding feasibility tolerances do not alone prevent repeated bases; finiteness needs an additional well-founded ordering or explicit nonrepetition mechanism.
assumptions_latex: The pivot test may accept steps using the current expanded feasibility tolerance.
No independent lexicographic or nonrepetition discipline is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implication \(\Delta_{k+1}>\Delta_k\Rightarrow B_{k+1}\notin\{B_0,\\ldots,B_k\}\) is not justified.
review_flags: The exact EXPAND variant and a published cycling construction must be sourced before strengthening this boundary to an existence theorem.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Rule Performance Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finiteness gives a combinatorial, generally exponential, pivot bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a standard-form linear program with \(m\) linearly independent equations and \(n\) variables, suppose a pivot discipline never revisits a basis and each iteration changes one basis. Moreover, enforcing lexicographic comparisons or symbolic perturbations may add work per ratio test; finiteness alone supplies no polynomial total-operation guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance-Induced Ties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerically indistinguishable ratio-test values form a tolerance tie set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_i\) be the eligible ratio-test values and \(r_* = \min_i r_i\). Thus the apparent nonuniqueness is created by the comparison threshold rather than by equality of the exact ratios.

children.title: Basis-Status Misclassification
children.top_down_role: Inconsistent basic, nonbasic, or bound classifications near tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Status Misclassification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Overlapping bound tolerances can assign incompatible variable statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bounded variable with \(l_i\le x_i\le u_i\), classify it as lower-active when \(x_i-l_i\le\tau_i\) and upper-active when \(u_i-x_i\le\tau_i\). If \(u_i-l_i\le2\tau_i\), both predicates can hold simultaneously. Unless basis membership and bound status are resolved by a consistent priority rule, the variable may be recorded as basic, lower-nonbasic, and upper-nonbasic by different tests. A sufficient separation condition preventing this overlap is \(u_i-l_i>2\tau_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a variable’s bound interval is no wider than twice its tolerance, lower- and upper-bound tests can both succeed and produce inconsistent statuses.

children.title: Finite Pivot Rules
children.top_down_role: Pivot disciplines classified by guaranteed basis-sequence termination.

assumptions_latex: Every instance in \(\mathcal{L}\) admits at least one starting basis satisfying the rule's stated admissibility requirements.
Every pivot selected at a nonterminal iteration is an admissible simplex pivot.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finiteness excludes every infinite basis sequence permitted by the rule on \(\mathcal{L}\), but it imposes no polynomial bound on the number of pivots.

notation.meaning: Specified class of feasible linear programs admitting the required starting bases.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{L}\) be a class of feasible linear programs for which the simplex method has at least one admissible starting basis. A simplex pivot rule is finite on \(\mathcal{L}\) if, for every instance in \(\mathcal{L}\), every basis sequence permitted by the rule from any admissible starting basis terminates after finitely many pivots with either an optimality certificate or an unboundedness certificate. If every instance in \(\mathcal{L}\) is bounded, the required terminal outcome is an optimal basis. This definition permits instance-dependent pivot counts and therefore does not imply a polynomial bound in the dimensions or input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pivot rule is finite on a specified feasible problem class when every basis sequence it permits from an admissible starting basis reaches a valid terminal outcome after finitely many exchanges; this does not imply polynomial complexity.

children.title: Polynomial Pivot-Rule Question
children.top_down_role: The complexity boundary between finite rules and polynomial pivot guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Pivot-Rule Question
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The question separating mere termination from polynomially many pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational linear programs encoded with bit length \(L\), the polynomial pivot-rule question asks whether there exists a simplex pivot rule and a polynomial \(p\) such that every admissible instance with \(m\) constraints and \(n\) variables terminates after at most \(p(m,n,L)\) pivots. A finite rule need only provide an instance-dependent finite count, such as the combinatorial bound \(\binom{n}{m}\); therefore finiteness alone does not answer the polynomial question.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polynomial pivot-rule question asks for a simplex rule whose pivot count is polynomial in dimensions and input length, a guarantee stronger than finiteness.
assumptions_latex: Input coefficients are rational and represented in a fixed binary encoding.
A pivot is counted as one simplex basis exchange.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite pivot rule is polynomial only if its worst-case pivot count admits a bound \(p(m,n,L)\).

children.title: Klee–Minty Families
children.top_down_role: Canonical distorted-cube constructions for long simplex paths.

assumptions_latex: The primal simplex method starts at the designated Klee--Minty vertex.
Dantzig's largest-positive-reduced-cost rule is used with the construction's prescribed variable ordering.

notation.meaning: A nondegenerate, recursively distorted d-dimensional cube with its Klee--Minty objective.
Number of simplex pivots made by Dantzig's rule.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Dantzig-rule lower-bound form; exact distortion parameters are omitted because equivalent normalizations occur in the literature.

source_refs.locator: 4. Worst-Case Analysis of the Simplex Method p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every dimension \(d\ge 1\), there is a nondegenerate bounded linear program whose feasible polytope \(K_d\) is combinatorially equivalent to the \(d\)-cube and whose objective orientation makes Dantzig's pivot rule follow a Hamiltonian path from the designated initial vertex to the unique optimum. Consequently, the rule visits all \(2^d\) vertices in path order and performs exactly \(2^d-1\) improving pivots. Thus an exponentially long simplex path can occur even when the feasible polytope is combinatorially a cube and every pivot is nondegenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Klee–Minty distorted cubes force Dantzig's rule through all 2^d vertices, requiring 2^d−1 pivots despite nondegeneracy and simple cube combinatorics.

children.title: Rule-Specific Exponential Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Long-path constructions distinguished by the affected pivot discipline.

assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a fixed deterministic simplex pivot rule.
\(I_d\) is a bounded linear program of dimension \(d\) with a designated initial basis.
The rule terminates at an optimal basis on every \(I_d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_R(I_d)\ge 2^{\alpha d}\) for some \(\alpha>0\) and infinitely many \(d\).

notation.meaning: Number of pivots selected by R on an instance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schema for a rule-specific exponential lower bound, not a claim that every pivot rule has such a known family.

source_refs.locator: 4. Worst-Case Analysis of the Simplex Method p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exponential lower bound for a specified pivot rule \(R\) consists of a constant \(\alpha>0\) and infinitely many dimensions \(d\) for which a bounded instance \(I_d\), together with its initial basis and all required tie-breaking conventions, satisfies \(L_R(I_d)\ge 2^{\alpha d}\). The construction is rule-specific: its conclusion concerns the path selected by \(R\), rather than every edge path or every simplex rule on \(I_d\). The input encoding and coefficient sizes must also be stated when the bound is interpreted as a bit-complexity lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rule-specific lower bound gives adversarial instances on which one named pivot rule, with fixed tie-breaking, takes exponentially many pivots.

children.title: Degeneracy-Amplified Worst Cases
children.top_down_role: Long or recurrent pivot behavior driven by degenerate basis structure.

assumptions_latex: The feasible linear program has at least one degenerate basic feasible solution.
Zero-length pivots are permitted by the pivot discipline.
No lexicographic or other proven anti-cycling rule is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{k+1}=x^k\) may hold at a pivot, and a repeated basis cycle may occur.

notation.meaning: The basic feasible solution represented after pivot k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates degeneracy-driven zero progress and cycling from nondegenerate exponential paths.

source_refs.locator: 5.7 Pivot Rules p. 71

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a degenerate basic feasible solution, the minimum-ratio test can return step length \(\theta=0\). The resulting pivot changes the basis while leaving both the primal point and objective value unchanged, so \(x^{k+1}=x^k\). Moreover, bounded linear programs exist for which admissible deterministic entering and leaving choices produce a finite sequence \(B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_q\) with \(B_q=B_0\), causing indefinite repetition. Hence strict objective improvement per pivot and finite termination do not follow from feasibility and boundedness alone; an anti-cycling discipline is required to exclude this mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degeneracy permits basis changes with zero primal and objective progress; without anti-cycling safeguards, admissible pivots can revisit a basis and cycle indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Amplified Worst Cases

children.title: Diameter-Pivot Path Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between existence of short edge paths and paths selected by a specific pivot rule.

children.title: Polyhedral Diameter Interface
children.top_down_role: The geometric availability of short vertex-to-vertex paths.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is a polytope.
\(G(P)\) is the undirected vertex-edge graph of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}_{G(P)}(u,v)\le \operatorname{diam}(P)\) for all vertices \(u,v\), but this does not bound a prescribed pivot rule's path by the same quantity.

notation.meaning: The undirected graph whose nodes are vertices of P and whose edges are polytope edges.
Shortest-path distance in the graph G(P).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected combinatorial diameter, distinguished from objective-monotone or rule-selected path length.

source_refs.locator: TWO: LINEAR ALGEBRA, CONVEX ANALYSIS, AND POLYHEDRAL SETS p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polytope \(P\), define its graph diameter by \[\operatorname{diam}(P)=\max_{u,v\in\operatorname{vert}(P)}\operatorname{dist}_{G(P)}(u,v),\] where \(G(P)\) is the undirected vertex-edge graph. This quantity guarantees the existence of an edge path of at most \(\operatorname{diam}(P)\) edges between every pair of vertices. It does not assert that the path is monotone for a chosen objective, begins with a prescribed basis, or is selected by a specified pivot rule; those additional restrictions can produce a longer path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyhedral diameter is the maximum shortest undirected edge distance between vertices; it guarantees short paths exist but does not control a pivot rule's choices.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Diameter Interface

source_witnesses.locator: TWO: LINEAR ALGEBRA, CONVEX ANALYSIS, AND POLYHEDRAL SETS p. 45

children.title: Pivot-Rule Path Length
children.top_down_role: The algorithmically selected path length under a specified pivot rule.

assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a fully specified pivot rule, including tie-breaking.
The simplex run starts from basis \(B_0\) and terminates first at an optimal basis \(B_T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_R(I,B_0)=T\), the number of pivot transitions before first optimality.

notation.meaning: Pivot-rule path length from the prescribed initial basis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts basis transitions, including degenerate pivots, until the first optimal basis.

source_refs.locator: 5.7 Pivot Rules p. 71

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an instance \(I\), initial basis \(B_0\), and fully specified pivot rule \(R\), let \(B_{k+1}\) be the basis selected from \(B_k\) by one application of \(R\). If \(B_T\) is the first optimal basis reached, define \[L_R(I,B_0)=T.\] Every basis transition counts, including a degenerate pivot that leaves the primal point unchanged. If the rule cycles or otherwise never reaches an optimal basis, set \(L_R(I,B_0)=+\infty\). This rule-selected length is generally different from the shortest graph distance to an optimal vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pivot-rule path length counts all basis changes from a prescribed start until first optimality, including degenerate pivots; nontermination gives infinite length.
knowledge_statements.title: Pivot-Rule Path Length

children.title: Beyond-Worst-Case Pivot Analysis
children.top_down_role: Distributional and perturbation-based models for simplex pivot performance.

children.title: Average-Case Pivot Analysis
children.top_down_role: Expected pivot behavior under specified input distributions.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is sampled from a specified probability distribution \(\mathcal{D}\).
The initial-basis and tie-breaking conventions are measurable functions of the sampled instance.
\(L_R(I)\) is a nonnegative extended random variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}_{I\sim\mathcal{D}}[L_R(I)]\) is the average-case pivot count, when the expectation is finite.

notation.meaning: Pivot count of rule R on the sampled instance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional expectation over instances, distinct from empirical sample averages and randomized-rule expectation on a fixed instance.

source_refs.locator: 5. Empirical Average Performance of the Simplex Method p. 50

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed pivot rule \(R\) and an explicitly specified distribution \(\mathcal{D}\) over encoded linear-program instances, the average-case pivot count is \[A_R(\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{I\sim\mathcal{D}}[L_R(I)].\] The distribution must include any random initial basis or preprocessing convention. If \(R\) is itself randomized, the joint expectation is \(\mathbb{E}_{I\sim\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{\omega}[L_R(I;\omega)]\), where \(\omega\) denotes the rule's internal randomness. An average-case statement is meaningful only relative to this probability model and does not imply a worst-case bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average-case analysis is the expected pivot count under an explicit instance distribution, optionally averaged again over a pivot rule's internal randomness.

children.title: Randomized Pivot Rules
children.top_down_role: Random-edge and randomized candidate-selection families.

assumptions_latex: A feasible nonoptimal basis \(B_k\) is available.
The set \(E_k\) of eligible improving pivots is finite and nonempty.
A probability distribution \(p_k\) on \(E_k\) is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The next pivot \(e_k\) is sampled according to \(p_k\), and iteration stops when \(E_k=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Eligible improving pivots at iteration k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical random-edge form; randomized candidate-subset rules arise by changing the distribution-generating step.

source_refs.locator: 5.7 Pivot Rules p. 71

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a linear program and a feasible initial basis \(B_0\). At iteration \(k\), form the finite set \(E_k\) of admissible improving pivots from \(B_k\). If \(E_k=\varnothing\), stop and output \(B_k\). Otherwise choose a distribution \(p_k\) satisfying \(p_k(e)\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{e\in E_k}p_k(e)=1\), sample \(e_k\sim p_k\), and pivot to \(B_{k+1}\). Random-edge uses \(p_k(e)=1/|E_k|\); randomized candidate-selection rules first sample or construct a subset and then select within it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized pivot rule samples an eligible improving pivot from a specified iteration-dependent distribution; random-edge uses the uniform distribution over improving edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Pivot Rules

children.title: Smoothed Simplex Analysis
children.top_down_role: Pivot behavior under small random perturbations of arbitrary instances.

assumptions_latex: The normalized encoded instance \(I\) satisfies \(\|I\|\le 1\).
The perturbation \(Z_\sigma\) has a stated distribution and scale \(\sigma>0\).
The simplex rule \(R\), initialization, and tie-breaking are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_R(d,\sigma)=\sup_{\|I\|\le 1}\mathbb{E}[L_R(I+Z_\sigma)]\) measures smoothed pivot complexity.

notation.meaning: Random coefficient perturbation at scale sigma.
Worst expected pivot count after perturbing a normalized d-dimensional instance.
Pivot count of the fixed simplex rule.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General smoothed-complexity functional; Gaussian coefficient perturbations are a common but not universal specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a normalized class of dimension-\(d\) linear-program encodings, a pivot rule \(R\), and a perturbation model \(Z_\sigma\) of magnitude \(\sigma>0\). The smoothed pivot complexity is represented by \[S_R(d,\sigma)=\sup_{\|I\|\le 1}\mathbb{E}_{Z_\sigma}\![L_R(I+Z_\sigma)\].\] The supremum preserves an adversarial choice of the center instance \(I\), while the expectation averages over its random perturbation. Any bound on \(S_R\) must state which coefficients are perturbed, their distribution, the normalization norm, and how infeasible or ill-posed perturbed instances are handled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smoothed analysis takes the worst center instance but averages the pivot count after a specified small random perturbation of its encoded coefficients.

children.title: Practical Pivot-Rule Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Solver-facing performance measures that balance iterations against computational and numerical cost.

children.title: Pivot-Count Cost Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: The central iteration-count and per-iteration-cost comparison.

children.title: Simplex Pivot Count
children.top_down_role: Iteration-count behavior associated with a pivot policy.

assumptions_latex: A simplex run produces bases \(B_0,B_1,\ldots\).
The stopping convention is first arrival at an optimal basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{piv}}=\inf\{k\ge 0:B_k\text{ is optimal}\}\), with value \(+\infty\) if no such basis occurs.

notation.meaning: Total number of completed pivots before first optimality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An algorithmic count of basis transitions, not arithmetic work or the number of distinct vertices.

source_refs.locator: 5.7 Pivot Rules p. 71

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a simplex execution with initial basis \(B_0\), define the pivot count by \[N_{\mathrm{piv}}=\inf\{k\ge 0:B_k\text{ is optimal}\}.\] Thus \(N_{\mathrm{piv}}=0\) when the initial basis is already optimal, and every completed basis exchange increases the count by one. Degenerate pivots count even when the primal point and objective value do not change. If no optimal basis is reached, set \(N_{\mathrm{piv}}=+\infty\). Revisited bases are counted on every occurrence, so this quantity need not equal the number of distinct bases or vertices encountered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simplex pivot count is the number of basis exchanges completed before first optimality, counting degenerate and repeated-basis pivots; nontermination gives infinity.

children.title: Work per Simplex Pivot
children.top_down_role: Computational effort incurred during an individual pivot iteration.

assumptions_latex: The revised simplex method maintains a basis matrix \(B_k\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\).
Arithmetic work is measured in scalar operations.
The factorization-update and pricing implementations are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_k=W_k^{\mathrm{price}}+W_k^{\mathrm{ratio}}+W_k^{\mathrm{update}}+W_k^{\mathrm{misc}}\).

notation.meaning: Arithmetic work performed during pivot k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational decomposition for revised simplex; asymptotic terms depend on sparsity, factorization, and pricing strategy.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For pivot \(k\) of a revised-simplex implementation, decompose its arithmetic work as \[W_k=W_k^{\mathrm{price}}+W_k^{\mathrm{ratio}}+W_k^{\mathrm{update}}+W_k^{\mathrm{misc}},\] where the terms respectively cover reduced-cost pricing, direction and ratio-test operations, basis-factorization maintenance, and remaining bookkeeping. The value of \(W_k\) is implementation-dependent: dense refactorization may require cubic work in \(m\), while factorization updates and sparse solves can be substantially cheaper. Consequently, a pivot rule that performs more pricing or produces unfavorable updates can increase per-pivot work even if it reduces the pivot count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Work per pivot combines pricing, ratio-test, basis-update, and bookkeeping costs, whose sizes depend on sparsity, numerical linear algebra, and the pivot rule.

children.title: Total-Work Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Interaction between iteration quantity versus per-iteration expense.

assumptions_latex: The run terminates after \(N_{\mathrm{piv}}<\infty\) pivots.
Each pivot has nonnegative measured work \(W_k\).
Initialization and finalization require work \(W_{\mathrm{fixed}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_{\mathrm{total}}=W_{\mathrm{fixed}}+\sum_{k=0}^{N_{\mathrm{piv}}-1}W_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact accounting identity under a declared work metric; it explains why pivot count alone is incomplete.

source_refs.locator: 5.7 Pivot Rules p. 71

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under a fixed arithmetic, memory-access, or elapsed-time cost model, the total work of a terminating simplex run is \[W_{\mathrm{total}}=W_{\mathrm{fixed}}+\sum_{k=0}^{N_{\mathrm{piv}}-1}W_k.\] Hence minimizing \(N_{\mathrm{piv}}\) does not necessarily minimize \(W_{\mathrm{total}}\): a rule may spend more work on pricing or factorization maintenance at each iteration in exchange for fewer pivots. If constants \(w_{\min}\) and \(w_{\max}\) satisfy \(0<w_{\min}\le W_k\le w_{\max}\), then \(W_{\mathrm{fixed}}+w_{\min}N_{\mathrm{piv}}\le W_{\mathrm{total}}\le W_{\mathrm{fixed}}+w_{\max}N_{\mathrm{piv}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total simplex work is fixed overhead plus the sum of per-pivot costs, so fewer pivots need not mean less computation when pivots differ in cost.
